verdict.rationale: The lexical pattern cleanly supports two of the proposition's three claims and leaves the middle claim genuinely contested. Testing is commanded with explicit verbs: 'test' (dokimazete) in 1 Thessalonians 5:21, 'test the spirits' (dokimazete ta pneumata) in 1 John 4:1, and 'let the others weigh' (diakrinetosan) in 1 Corinthians 14:29. Closure of the prophetic book is also explicit ('add to' (epitithemi) and 'take away' (aphaireo) in Revelation 22:18-19). The middle claim, that any retained modern prophecy is never binding the way Scripture is, is materially contested because the same noun 'prophecy' (propheteia, G4394) and the same agent noun 'prophet' (prophetes, G4396) are used in one single sense (univocally) for Old Testament prophets, New Testament writing prophets, and New Testament congregational prophets (1 Corinthians 14:29, 32, 37; Ephesians 2:20; Ephesians 3:5; Acts 21:10), and the Agabus oracle (Acts 21:11) names binders the words do not perfectly match in the outcome (Acts 21:33), so the canon supplies two patterns the words do not rank: a binary Old Testament prophet test (Deuteronomy 18:22) and a gradated New Testament sift-and-hold instruction. Therefore disputed.

scripture.reasoning: The clause 'do not despise prophecies' (propheteias me exoutheneite) treats prophetic utterance as a category not to be discarded wholesale, presupposing speech that has continuing value and must be received before it is weighed. The noun 'prophecy' (propheteia) is the same word (lemma) used for the words of the book of Revelation (Revelation 22:18-19) and for the prophetic Scripture of 2 Peter 1:20-21.

'Test all things, hold fast the good' (panta de dokimazete, to kalon katechete) commands an assaying of every utterance and selective retention of the good. The verb 'to test, to prove' (dokimazo, G1381) denotes proving or assaying metal and is used twenty-two times in the New Testament, including 1 John 4:1 ('test the spirits', dokimazete ta pneumata), Romans 12:2, and Ephesians 5:10. It entails a sift in which some content is kept and the rest released. This supports the testing claim but presents a gradated model rather than a binary accept-or-execute model.

'Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh, distinguish' (prophetai de duo e treis laleitosan, kai hoi alloi diakrinetosan). The verb 'to weigh, to distinguish' (diakrino, G1252) means to judge between, distinguish, evaluate, and is used nineteen times in the New Testament for discerning food (Acts 11:12), discerning the body (1 Corinthians 11:29), and self-examination. The imperative directs the congregation to weigh prophetic utterance piece by piece, the same gradated sift posture as 1 Thessalonians 5:21.

'If anyone thinks he is a prophet or spiritual, let him recognize that what I write to you is the Lord's command' (ei tis dokei prophetes einai e pneumatikos, epiginosketo ha grapho hymin hoti kyriou estin entole). Paul applies 'prophet' (prophetes, G4396) to the same congregational figures of 14:29 and then asserts that his own written word is 'the Lord's command' (kyriou entole), which in the vocabulary itself subordinates congregational 'prophecy' (propheteia) to apostolic 'writing, Scripture' (graphe) within the same chapter, supplying a real data point for an authority gradient.

'Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world' (me panti pneumati pisteuete, alla dokimazete ta pneumata ei ek tou theou estin, hoti polloi pseudoprophetai exelelythasin eis ton kosmon). The imperative 'test' (dokimazete) is the same verb as 1 Thessalonians 5:21, applied to spirits and to 'false prophets' (pseudoprophetai), confirming that the testing posture is spread across the whole Bible (pan-canonical) and that spurious prophetic claims are an expected hazard.

The 'prophet' (nabi, H5030) who speaks a word in YHWH's name that He did not command, or who speaks in the name of other gods, must die. The ETCBC clause-function tags here (from a Hebrew Bible syntax database) mark patterns of Predicate, Complement, and Negation characteristic of a legal 'if X then Y' apodosis (the 'then' clause of a conditional law). The death sentence makes the standard for a claimed prophet absolute, not gradated, with no surviving partial authority.

The clause 'how shall we know the word that the LORD has not spoken' (eka neda et hadabar asher lo dibbero YHWH) frames the chapter as supplying a test of authenticity, a recognition that not every claim to a divine word is genuine.

'The word does not happen and does not come to pass' (lo yihyeh hadabar velo yavo) is the fulfillment test: a word that fails verification was not from YHWH and the speaker is not to be feared. The standard is non-fulfillment equals false, a binary verdict with no surviving partial authority. This is the Old Testament prophet test cited at Deuteronomy 13:1-5 and reapplied in Jeremiah 28 and Ezekiel 13.

Agabus, called 'prophet' (prophetes, G4396) in v. 10, says 'thus the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man whose belt this is, and deliver him into the hands of the gentiles' (houtos ton andra hou estin he zone haute houtos desousin (G1210 'to bind', deo) en Ierousalem hoi Ioudaioi (G2453, 'the Jews') kai paradosousin (G3860 'to hand over', paradidomi) eis cheiras ethnon). The verb 'bind' (deo) and the action 'hand over, deliver' (paradidomi) are anchored to the Jews as agent of binding and to delivery to gentiles as a separate act.

The chiliarch (Roman commander of a thousand) 'took hold of him' (epelabeto autou, G1949) 'and commanded' (kai ekeleusen, G2753 'to command', keleuo) 'him to be bound' (dethenai, G1210 'to bind', deo) 'with two chains' (halysesi (G0254 'chain') dysi). The binder is the Roman commander not the Jews, and the binding is by Roman chains. The verb 'bind' (deo) matches Agabus' verb but the agent does not match 'the Jews' (hoi Ioudaioi) of v. 11. This is a real near-miss in the vocabulary that the schema must record honestly: the prediction is largely fulfilled but not precisely, which weighs against Agabus' utterance meeting the binary Deuteronomy 18:22 fulfillment standard while still being treated by Luke as a true prophetic warning.

'Built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets' (epoikodomethentes epi to themelio ton apostolon kai propheton). The 'of the prophets' (ton propheton) form uses G4396 (the same word as Acts 21:10 of Agabus and 1 Corinthians 14:29 of congregational prophets) coordinated with 'of the apostles' (apostolon), placing some class of New Testament prophets at the church's foundation. Whether this refers to Old Testament prophets, New Testament writing prophets, or includes the same congregational figures of 1 Corinthians 14 is contested by the words alone.

'Now revealed to His holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit' (nyn apekalyphthe tois hagiois apostolois autou kai prophetais en pneumati). The adverb 'now' (nyn) and the coordination with 'to the apostles' (apostolois) locate these 'prophets' (prophetai, G4396) in the new-covenant era, but the word by itself does not rank their utterances relative to apostolic 'writing, Scripture' (graphe).

'If anyone adds to them' (ean tis epithei ep auta) attaches a curse of plagues to adding to 'the words of the prophecy of this book' (tous logous tes propheteias tou bibliou toutou). The prohibition is against augmenting the fixed prophetic word and uses the same word 'prophecy' (propheteia, G4394) used in 1 Thessalonians 5:20 and 1 Corinthians 13:2.

'And if anyone takes away from the words' (kai ean tis aphelei apo ton logon) threatens removal from the tree of life and the holy city for subtracting from the prophetic words of the book. Adding and subtracting are both forbidden, fixing the word as closed and non-augmentable.

'All Scripture is God-breathed' (pasa graphe theopneustos) and useful 'for teaching, for reproof, for correction' (pros didaskalian, pros elegmon, pros epanorthosin). 'God-breathed' (theopneustos) predicates a unique divine origin of 'Scripture' (graphe), which establishes Scripture as the norming standard (the rule by which other claims are measured) against which other claims are measured.

'That the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work' (hina artios e ho tou theou anthropos, pros pan ergon agathon exertismenos). 'Complete' (artios, a word that occurs only once in the entire New Testament, a hapax) and 'fully equipped' (exertismenos) assert sufficiency of Scripture for the equipping it describes, but the clause is purposive (a 'so that' or 'in order that' clause) and does not by itself pronounce on whether other revelatory speech could coexist as non-norming (not functioning as the rule).

complicating_texts.resolution: The provision that a seated prophet yield when 'a revelation' (apokalypsis) comes to another ('but if a revelation should come to another seated' (ean de allo apokalyphthe kathemeno)) assumes ongoing congregational revelatory speech in the apostolic assembly. The noun 'revelation' (apokalypsis, G0602) is the same word used for the revelation of Jesus Christ in Revelation 1:1 and Galatians 1:12. The word does not by itself rank such 'revelation' (apokalypsis) relative to apostolic 'writing, Scripture' (graphe), so its existence does not settle the bindingness question but does establish that ongoing revelatory speech was a normal apostolic-era category.

Disciples at Tyre tell Paul 'through the Spirit' (dia tou pneumatos) not to 'step on, set foot in' (epibainein) Jerusalem, yet Paul proceeds and Luke does not treat him as disobedient. The construction is a Spirit-prompted utterance directed against an apostolic itinerary that the apostle nevertheless overrides. In the vocabulary this records a category of Spirit-mediated speech that did not function as absolutely binding even on its own apostolic hearer, which is a real data point on the disputed side of the bindingness question.

Agabus is named 'prophet' (prophetes, G4396), the same word (lemma) as Old Testament prophets and as the congregational prophets of 1 Corinthians 14. The shared term is the lexical source of the dispute: if the same word names both Isaiah and Agabus and the 1 Corinthians 14 weighers, the canon supplies no built-in vocabulary distinction between binding revelatory prophecy and gradated congregational prophecy.

Agabus predicts that 'the Jews' (hoi Ioudaioi) will 'bind' (deo) Paul and 'deliver' (paradidomi) him to the gentiles. In Acts 21:33 the Roman chiliarch (Roman commander of a thousand) is the one who orders the binding 'with chains' (halysesi), and the Jews are the mob attempting to kill him. The predicted verb 'bind' (deo) is fulfilled; the predicted agent (the Jews) does not strictly match the actual agent (the Romans). On the binary Deuteronomy 18:22 standard this would be a problematic inexactness; yet Luke clearly presents Agabus as a true prophet. This is the principal data point in the vocabulary that some readers cite for a category of true but not infallibly precise prophecy.

'The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets' (pneumata propheton prophetais hypotassetai). The verb 'to be subject to, to be under the control of' (hypotasso, G5293) under a linking verb 'is' (copula) construction asserts that prophetic spirits are under the control of prophets, presupposing that congregational prophetic utterance is not an overwhelming irresistible word but a controllable, weighable speech. This argues for the gradated New Testament model but does not by itself foreclose a binding category.

Foundational 'prophets' (prophetai, G4396) coordinated with 'apostles' (apostoloi) at the church's foundation. Whether this names Old Testament prophets, a distinct class of New Testament writing prophets, or the same congregational figures of 1 Corinthians 14 is not settled by the word alone. The unresolved referent is itself part of why the bindingness comparison is disputed at the level of the original-language vocabulary.

variants.note: Revelation 22:18-19 carries apparatus marks in the bundle surface (the diple symbols (editorial marks flagging textual variation) on 'he will add' (epithesei) and 'he will take away' (aphelei) reflect editorial variation between 'take away' (aphele) and 'will take away' (aphelei)), but the lexical verdict does not turn on these readings. The addition or subtraction prohibition stands across the variant forms. New Testament passages outside 3 John are in ecm-shadow status (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants, the ECM apparatus, has not yet been fully published for them).

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads 2 Timothy 3:16-17 sufficiency ('God-breathed Scripture' (theopneustos graphe), 'complete' (artios), 'fully equipped' (exertismenos)) and Revelation 22:18-19 closure ('add to' (epitithemi) and 'take away' (aphaireo) on the words of the prophecy) as terminating revelatory prophecy with the close of the apostolic period, so any modern claim is by definition non-binding and to be rejected if it adds to Scripture. On this reading 1 Thessalonians 5:21 and 1 Corinthians 14:29 belong to a transitional apostolic-era practice now ceased.

Reads 1 Thessalonians 5:20-21 ('test', dokimazete), 1 Corinthians 14:29 ('let the others weigh', diakrinetosan), 1 John 4:1 ('test the spirits', dokimazete ta pneumata), and 1 Corinthians 14:30-32 ('is subject', hypotassetai; 'revelation', apokalypsis) as instituting an ongoing sift-and-retain prophecy distinct in authority from apostolic 'writing, Scripture' (graphe). The Agabus near-miss (Acts 21:11 vs 21:33) and the Acts 21:4 override are read as data points in the vocabulary that New Testament congregational prophecy could be genuine yet not infallibly precise. On this lens the testing and no-addition claims hold, but the absolute never-binding claim requires qualification because retained good is to be 'held fast' (katechete).

Reads the noun 'prophet' (prophetes, G4396) as carrying a single binding sense across canon, so that Agabus, the 1 Corinthians 14 prophets, the Ephesians 2:20 foundation prophets, and Old Testament 'prophet' (nabi) all stand under the same Deuteronomy 18:22 standard. On this reading, genuine prophecy that survives the test is by definition binding, but it is also by definition rare and tested. The proposition is affirmed but its third clause is read as redundant once any non-genuine word is sifted out.

competing_lens_verdicts.framework: old testament prophet standard applied univocally
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads Deuteronomy 18:20-22 as the controlling test for any prophetic claim: non-fulfillment equals false, with no surviving partial authority. Applied in one single sense (univocally) to modern claims this affirms the proposition. Its univocal transfer to New Testament congregational prophecy is itself the disputed step, since the New Testament words ('test', dokimazo; 'weigh, distinguish', diakrino) describe a gradated rather than binary process.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on whether the Old Testament binary prophet test (Deuteronomy 18) and the New Testament sift-and-hold instruction (1 Thessalonians 5:21, 1 Corinthians 14:29, 1 John 4:1) describe one standard or two distinct orders of prophecy. The anchor words establish that testing is commanded and that the canonical prophetic word may not be augmented, but they do not by themselves resolve the relative authority question. The same words 'prophecy' (propheteia) and 'prophet' (prophetes) are used in one single sense (univocally) for Old Testament and New Testament prophets, which is a real pressure in the vocabulary on the proposition's middle claim. progressive_revelation is set true because the relationship between Old Testament and New Testament prophetic categories is itself part of the dispute.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Modern claims to prophecy are to be evaluated against Scripture. The question is whether any such claim, once evaluated, carries an authority equal to, lesser than, or other than the written Scripture, and whether revelation that adds to or contradicts Scripture is to be received.
stem_audit.notes: The phrase 'binding on conscience the way Scripture is' embeds a comparative norming claim (Scripture as the final conscience-binding standard) that is the contested matter, not a neutral premise. The clause 'new revelation that adds to or contradicts Scripture is rejected' also presupposes a closed-canon conclusion. The testing and no-addition portions are lexically supported. VERDICT-CHANGED: The verdict is derived on the original stem and lands as disputed because of the comparative bindingness claim and because 'prophecy' (propheteia) and 'prophet' (prophetes) are used in one single sense (univocal lemmas) across canon.

lay_summary: This proposition makes three claims: that modern prophecy must be tested by Scripture, that it is never binding the way Scripture is, and that revelation adding to or contradicting Scripture is rejected. The original-language evidence cleanly supports the first and third. The verb 'test' (dokimazete) is used in 1 Thessalonians 5 and 1 John 4 for testing utterances and spirits, and in 1 Corinthians 14 the verb 'let the others weigh' (diakrinetosan) commands the same sifting of prophetic speech. Revelation 22 forbids both 'adding' (epitithemi) and 'taking away' (aphaireo) from the words of the prophecy of the book, fixing the word as closed. 2 Timothy 3 calls all Scripture 'God-breathed' (theopneustos) and sufficient to equip the man of God. So the testing claim and the no-addition claim rest on firm ground in the original-language vocabulary. The middle claim is where the words stop short of a single answer. Two facts in the text drive the dispute. First, the noun 'prophecy' (propheteia) and the agent noun 'prophet' (prophetes) are the same words (lemmas) used for Isaiah, for the writing prophets of Revelation, for the foundation prophets of Ephesians 2, and for the congregational prophets weighed in 1 Corinthians 14. The canon supplies no built-in vocabulary that ranks one of these as binding and another as gradated. Second, Agabus in Acts 21 is called 'prophet' (prophetes) and predicts that the Jews will 'bind' (deo) Paul and 'deliver' (paradidomi) him to the gentiles, but in the same chapter the Romans not the Jews do the binding, with Roman chains. The verb of binding matches; the agent does not strictly match. Some readers take this near-miss in the vocabulary as evidence that genuine New Testament prophecy could be true in substance without meeting the binary Deuteronomy 18 fulfillment standard. Other readers take it as a reason to confine genuine binding prophecy to a closed apostolic-era category. The words themselves do not rank these two readings. The verdict is therefore disputed: two of the three claims are lexically secure, while the comparative claim about how binding retained prophecy is depends on a reading the words permit but do not compel.
